Title: Evil plays and other random acts of violence

Messages.Author: Tim Eijpe
Messages.Body:
Hi all.
In one of our weekly gamenights we decided to play 3 rounds with the same
deck
in a semi-tourney way. Now we played 2 prelims and one "final".
As I swept in the first round I thought: hell I will not need more VP, but
was
a bit afraid by my predators deck, heavy combat (o VP at that moment). My
deck
would not be very good against it, but my prey had the anti deck, heavy
prevention (all hail seating order).
So to increase the chances of not facing the combat deck in the "finals" I
declared withdrawel on my first turn as there were no weenie deck at the
table. So I got one VP (kept mine) and decreased the pool of VPs at the
table.
But is this legal? I dunno, though it is kind of unsportsmanlike...

Any ideas?

Tim

I'm ambivalent about that. I can understand it but retaliation in this case
really has no point and it's easier to conclude it was done for other
reasons. My point is that against any smart player it's nearly impossible to
prove collusion even if it existed. You can always blame it on all kinds of
things, like the case above where you'd say it was for retaliation when it
maybe really was only to prevent him from goingto the final or even worse,
to help your friend to gain a VP just because he's your friend.

Personally I rarely retaliate like that evne in friendly games (but it

his job and I have nothing to gain by playing the AI and ruin the game for

Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
"Jason Bell" <Jason...@mail.com>

> Retaliation against the methuselah who is ousting you
> is definitely an in-game consideration.
>
> One of my favorites, actually.

I'm not sure about this...

If you will be ousted regardless of what you do, retaliating at that point
seems petty and unsportsmanlike. I guess this depends on the scenario, but
there is a fine line between trying to win and trying to cause someone else
to lose.

The situation Roger Carhult mentioned regarding the playing of Archon
Investigation to self-oust rather than taking a bleed which will also oust,
while legal, is also somewhat obnoxious IMHO.

I think it's natural to lash out like that, but it doesn't serve anyone. As
soon as you are ousted you should be offering your hand to your predator and
prey, not making sure your predator has a rougher ride finishing the game.

I had a problem a few months back with one player whose style of play was
not to try to win but to constantly attack me from wherever he sat with
cards like Night Moves, rushes, you name it. For him, the game was not 'Oust
your prey' or 'Win at Jyhad' but 'Attack Wes'. I don't mind this if it's
logical and serves the greater goal (though this is sometimes difficult to
determine)... in this case it clearly wasn't--he admitted it. That's old
news however... He has since improved in this capacity and almost made it to
the finals when we were in Toronto in May.

I don't know how much any of you consider trying to manipulate the
tournament so that certain decks make it or don't make it to the finals
table... At the two tournaments I have attended this was not something that
I personally ever considered. It was far more relevant to me to get *to* the
finals. To the best of my knowledge, nobody ever tried to prevent another
player from getting to the finals. I can see an advantage to doing this but
it seems a bit shady... but maybe that's just me.

Even writing this it seems to me that certain groups have different
standards as far as keeping deals and sportsmanlike behaviour etc. While I
understand that a certain amount of Machiavellian behaviour is required (and
fun!) in Jyhad, I've also seen behaviour that is unnecessarily ruthless and
insulting to other players. If I can't call the people I'm playinig with
friends after a Jyhad match, I'm not sure that they're the kind of players I
want to play with... know what I mean? This is rare though and I'm talking
about fairly extreme cases.

Cheers,
WES

Why is it more noble to lie down for your predator, making his job
against your prey easier? I believe that if the math shows I'm to
be ousted with no recourse, I work to make the job tougher, not
easier.

If I follow your argument correctly (or intentionally misconstrue
your argument for my own purposes), I, as a good sport with
1 pool, should always let the first minion oust me if it is clear
that I cannot block the last minion. If so, I am a poor sport
indeed, as I block with everything I have, sending as many
opposing minions to torpor or otherwise mistreating them
until my last minion has blocked his second to last.

The most frustrated I've been playing in my group is when
a player just quits in such a position, influencing himself to death
or otherwise not trying to stay and fight. To me, that's much more
about not being a sport than the situation with the Archon
Investigation.

But then again, it's been a loooooong time since anyone has
accused me of not being sufficiently competitive.

- Jason Bell

"Unique Master. Gain a master phase action and put this card into
play. Tap to move two blood from the blood bank to a ready vampire you
control. At the end of your turn, your predator takes control of The
Coven."

A literal reading would mean that

(a) you may tap the card to move two blood from the blood bank, etc.

*AND*

(b) at the end of your turn, your predator takes control, etc.

since (b) has no text specifying conditional with regards to (a), then
whether or not you tap The Coven, your predator will take control of
it.

Unlike, for example, Anarch Troublemaker, which reads:

"Unique Master. During your untap phase, you may tap up to two
vampires your prey controls or burn a piece of equipment belonging to
a minion your prey controls. If this is done, your prey takes control
of the Troublemaker. Burn Troublemaker if his or her controller is
ousted from the game."

...and uses the "If this is done" wording.

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Jason Bell
Messages.Body:
"Roger Carhult" <rogc...@student.luth.se> wrote

Your philosophy seems to preclude retaliation in most cases,
once something is done, at least when there is no chance
of that happening again (in this case, ousted is ousted,
and we all agree that no retaliation will make you more
ousted or less ousted).

I once played a game where I had to diablerize my predator's
vampire to stabilize my board position, and my grandprey's
voters burned my diablerist. I retaliated by burning down
his hunting ground, stealing one of his intercept retainers,
and assuring my prey that he should not be afraid to tap
out to bleed the guy.

I don't think I was being a poor sport, just demonstrating that
torching my vampires is not free (even though it was clear both
that I would do no more diablerizing that game and that my
retaliation would not make any future blood hunts fail).
In much this same sense, I don't think that the
ousted player was a poor sport by using AI to show that
ousting him was not free.

In the end, we may just be talking about different outlooks
in the game. I agree that what's done is done, but I will
always do what I can within the game to ensure that doing
it to me will be as expensive as I can make it.

I definitely would use the AI on my way out of the game,
probably every time, unless there were some other consideration,
like if I attributed my ouster more to my prey's upstream
interference than the final downstream bleed.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: Aaron
Messages.Body:
If collusion rules are to prevent you from doing something subjective,
whats the point? There is nothing to safe guard a player from being
"unsportman like" when in another city trying to screw over someone
else.

IE: next month I go to Ohio for Origins, the head judge there sees
that I am AI to burn my predators vampire as I am ousted. Since my
predator is from Ohio, and so are the judges it is in their minds to
agree with the guy they know...they have to see him next week. Since
the VEKN rules cannot provide for every instance they leave it up to
the judge. Sorry to lack faith in human logic(and pick on anyone from
Ohio) but there are no king solomans here.

Saying it's not advantagous for me to out my predator...someone across
table or whatever is foolish. Since your ultimate objective is to get
victory points, if you see someone cross table playing a deck that
is/could possibly screw you up later, it is your obligation to destroy
them, help their predator destroy them or what ever. And since
destroying everyone else, even backwards gains you 1 victory point for
last man standing...well 1 is still more then none isn't it? By not
AI my predators vampire when I have the chance always(even when I lose
because of it) I am in effect, agreeing to help him win. By letting
him keep his minions it is not benifitial to the player of the AI.

Or we can take LSJ's example. What if you justify your actions by
saying "maybe someone will save me with life boon!" What if, to that
remark, everyone says they don't have any. Then you are still playing
your AI with no hope of winning. In a game based on vampires, trying
to screw your oponent out of winning is just as good as trying to
contruct your own resources to win.

Fact is, if you are bleeding for more then 3...you deserve to be AIed
every time. Suck it up and take it on the chin...don't try to tell
the other player isn't not fair you big babies.

How about this:
If it is a 5 player game, and I have 2 VP for ousting 2 of my preys.
And now there are 3 of us left. Is it not up to me to make sure that
my predator does not sweep me and my prey? If he does he ends up with
3 VP, and if I am going to be taken out by my predator (which leaves
him with 1 VP and my prey with 0) shouldn't I AI his only minion
bleeing me, to make it easier for my prey to oust him? If my
objective is to end up with the most VP that ties me for the highest,
instead of losing to 3 for a sweep. So there I am, trying to fix the
VP at a table, but is that unfair? I put pressure on my predator even
by ousting myself, to make sure he doesn't end up with more then me.

What a great rule! You payed your money to get a shot at the prize - but
don't think about trying to get it using the rules you are given, because
that would be cheating.

Which line are you trying to draw? It seems you are trying to specify
which considerations are valid and which are not. Obviously not every
consideration should be valid, but why is "winning the tournament"
considered invalid when you're playing in a tournament?

: "Players must act only on in-game considerations."
: (VEKN Tournament Rules 5.2)

Is the round time-limit an in-game or out-of-game consideration? What
about a notorious player's style? What about regional metagame? What
about knowing what's in another player's deck from a previous round?
What about a player breaking a deal in the last round? Are we supposed to
pretend we don't have this information?

etc.), it shouldn't be contrary to the game's rules in the most critical of

comfortable changing the tournament rules than the game's rules.
